rows.en: The expression "a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai" is found in the book of the Mishnah three times,{v1_05_03:1} and in the book Torat Kohanim [Sifra] once, where it comprises three halakhot;{v1_05_03:2} in the Mekhilta and in the Sifre it is not mentioned at all. It occurs mostly in the other baraitot. In the Tosefta this expression is found only once, but its content is found in another form twice: "these are the very words that were spoken to Moses at Horeb." In the baraitot of the two Talmuds, the Yerushalmi and the Bavli, we find it seven times, but the particulars included in them are twenty in number.{v1_05_03:3} The Amoraim in the Talmud mentioned it fourteen times.{v1_05_03:4} The number of them all is forty-two. However, of all the halakhot found in the Mishnah, in Torat Kohanim and in the Tosefta under the name "a halakhah to Moses at Sinai," there is not even one on which all the sages agreed. This is a sign that those who say that they are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai did not say so relying on a clear tradition that was above all doubt; rather, they said so by way of conjecture, because these halakhot were doubtful to them, and their source, their cause and their reason were hidden from them. Therefore they attached them to the most ancient time, namely the time of the writing and the giving of the Torah, for that time was in any case the time of the beginning of tradition. It was established among them that the sense of several statutes in the Torah is not possible unless words of tradition preceded them, and likewise that the sense of some statutes of the Torah is not possible unless we determine that from their very beginning their explanation and their limits were clear and known. Therefore they supposed in their minds that all the halakhot that were doubtful with respect to their source and beginning were also received from the beginning of the Torah of Moses. Also of the halakhot mentioned in the baraita and in the sayings of the Amoraim, it was not said that they are halakhot to Moses at Sinai on the strength of an agreed tradition, for among all of them only sixteen are found on which no one disputes. And since there was no agreement of all the sages on most of the halakhot called by the name "a halakhah to Moses at Sinai," it follows necessarily that those who gave them this name also did so only by conjecture. Therefore who knows whether those halakhot too, on whose source and beginning no dispute is found, were not also attributed to Moses at Sinai only by conjecture? All the halakhot called by the name "a halakhah to Moses at Sinai" on whose attribution no one disputes, sixteen in number, concern the make-up of the tefillin and their form. They had a great reason to hold them as received, and also to proclaim especially that they are halakhot to Moses at Sinai. For it is clear that the sense of the scripture that was expounded as referring to the making of tefillin and to putting them on was the same for the ancient masters of scripture, who were the Sadducees, and for the masters of midrash. Although one can explain the scripture as a figure, in such a way that there is no commandment to make a sign and mark in deed, but that what is meant by the words "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes" [Deuteronomy 6:8] is only a figure of speech and a parable for keeping and remembering in the heart (Rashbam and Ibn Ezra), nevertheless all of them explained it as the making of tefillin, as an actual sign and binding. Even the Sadducees, who explained the words of the Torah as they are written, agreed to this explanation. For it follows for us from our Mishnah (Sanhedrin 88) that the commandment of tefillin as an actual act was counted as a matter written explicitly in the Torah, and that the Sadducees too agree to it (Horayot 4a). Therefore the belief was held among them that this commandment, in the way in which it was explained by the Scribes, was so explained from the time that this statute was given and written in the book. This being so, the act of the commandment and the form depend on each other. For we cannot picture to ourselves the act without determining the existence of some one form among the forms; and since in the Torah there is no hint of the form of the tefillin, necessarily their form was received among them orally. And this is the reason why they held all the halakhot concerning the form and make-up of the tefillin to be received from Moses at Sinai. And as for their taking special care to say publicly that these halakhot are from Sinai, they also had their reason for this: they wanted to show the great value that every small thing in this commandment has, and that every single part in the form of the tefillin has a source in a tradition from Sinai, because this commandment was weak in their hands at several times. Perhaps there really were in ancient days people who refused to explain the Torah in this direction, and did not explain its words as the giving of an actual sign and an actual binding. And even some of the first sages of the Torah, although they believed with all their heart that the intent of the commandment was actual tefillin, nevertheless thought that the purpose of the commandment is that the fear of the Lord and His commandments be always before their eyes (Josephus, *Antiquities*, part 1, book 4, chapter 8); and where this purpose can be reached by another means, one need not insist on this act. They said explicitly that one who puts on tefillin is as if he reads in the Torah, and whoever reads in the Torah is exempt from tefillin (Mekhilta Bo, chapter 17). Therefore, without doubt, views like these sometimes caused a slackening of hands from the act in practice. Against this slackening they strove to fight, and said: whoever recites the Shema without tefillin is as if he bears false witness against himself (Berakhot 14b). They poured out contempt and wrath enough on those who slacken their hands from this commandment, until they called them "sinners of Israel with their body" (Rosh Hashanah 17a); and they said: who is an am ha-arets? Whoever does not put on tefillin every day (Berakhot 47b). And it is well known how despised in their eyes was the man whom they held to be an am ha-arets (Pesahim 49a), and that they kept the utmost distance from him (there; Nedarim 20a; and in many places). This effort also speaks from within some aggadot that spread in the nation, such as this: that the Holy One, blessed be He, puts on tefillin every day (Berakhot 6a), and that the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses the knot of the tefillin (there). And of Michal the daughter of Saul and of other righteous women they told that they put on tefillin (Mekhilta Bo, chapter 17; Eruvin 96a; Yerushalmi Berakhot chapter 2). All this was to show the great value of the commandment, and against the slackening with which they slackened their hands from it. Therefore we understand why they took special care to give the form of the tefillin an ancient source reaching back to Moses at Sinai. In one place we find that they said of one halakhah, "so it was given to them" (Temurah 16a), and this wording shows that their intent is that it was so given to them from Sinai, and it is so stated in the Talmud; but if we look well there, we find that they spoke only by a conjecture whose basis is words of aggadah. Various matters are described in the Mishnah, the baraita and the Talmud by the name "halakhah" without more, and nothing is said in them about the nature and source of such halakhot. But the later [authorities] usually explain halakhot of this kind as also being ancient halakhot, and attribute them to Moses at Sinai.{v1_05_05:1} Sometimes the Gemara uses the expressions hilkheta gemiri, or gemara gemiri, or gemiri ["we have it by tradition"], and of all these expressions the commentators of the Talmud said that they refer to a halakhah to Moses at Sinai.{v1_05_05:2} And there are halakhot for which they used the expression "in truth" or "in truth they said," and of these too they said that they are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai.{v1_05_05:3} But if we look well at most of the places where all these expressions are mentioned, we find clearly and without any doubt that these phrases do not indicate a halakhah to Moses at Sinai in the precise sense.

After these words and this truth we can judge justly that in all the generations of the ancient sages, for whom most of the halakhot from the time before them were doubtful, and whose source and also reason were hidden from them, they attached them to the most ancient time. We shall not wonder at their doubts and at the first source being hidden from them, for so it lay in the nature of the matter. From the beginning, when they restored the religion to its former state in the days of Ezra, everything that was established and founded in the laws of the Torah was like a decree issued from before the ruler; all was by the agreement of all or most of them, and on the foundation of such an agreement every matter was concluded and became a fixed statute. But it was not written for the generations when, by whom and for what reason this statute was enacted; it became a practice in the midst of the people, and like a part of the Torah for the learners and the students, until it stood on one level with all the received statutes. It is self-evident that in the course of time, and especially from the time when study was held back by various events, they forgot and no longer knew how to distinguish between what was truly received from ancient days (perhaps as far back as the days when the Torah was given) and what the first Scribes derived by their understanding from the scripture or from reasoning. Therefore, as time went further on, so the doubt grew among them; and so it is no wonder that any matter that was doubtful, and whose source and reason they could not grasp, they held to be a matter received from the most ancient time, for in truth there lived and endured among them matters received from that time. And we find that the sages of the generations sometimes sought to give a reason and argument for the words of their predecessors, and their colleagues or those who came after them did not agree with them, because their reason and argument were not right in their eyes; and in this way they preferred to attach the matter to an ancient tradition and to hold it as a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, rather than to give it a reason that was in no way right in their eyes. And indeed it is wiser to hold a matter as an ancient tradition out of doubt and by way of conjecture (for then there is no danger of its abolition, since every received matter was holy to them like the words of the Torah) than to give it a reason and argument built on a shaky foundation, from which the danger of the complete abolition of the matter is near. In this way we saw that the first sages sought to give a reason for the willow and the water libation, and derived these halakhot from the scripture by a far-fetched and strange midrash; and those who came after them threw this reason away. Not that they gave another, more correct reason; rather, they decided that there is no need to search for a reason and cause, for these are halakhot received [as given] to Moses at Sinai. This is stated explicitly in the incident that happened to R. Akiva with his students (Niddah 45a), when R. Akiva sought to give a reason and argument for a doubtful halakhah. When he set out his argument and his reason before his students, they looked at him as men astonished at the matter, for his words were not right in their eyes; and they said to him: why should we seek a far-fetched reason with which our mind is not at ease? Is it not nearer to attach the doubtful [halakhah] to an ancient tradition and to say of it that it is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, just as we say that the whole Torah is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai? It is clear that they did not attach it to a tradition from Sinai because the matter was received among them; rather, they said so by way of analogy and conjecture. For how is it possible that the students had a tradition of a thing that their master had not handed down to them as a halakhah to Moses at Sinai? And just as we saw from the incident that happened to R. Akiva with his students that they sometimes attributed some halakhah to a tradition from the most ancient time, not because they had clear proof but only by conjecture, so it was with all the doubtful halakhot: even where they did not know the chain of tradition, and there was doubt about their source and their time, they attributed them to Moses at Sinai when they saw that the halakhah was agreed upon and rooted in the people. The way of speaking in exaggeration about the history of their time is not strange or remote for the sages of the Oral Torah, for so they said explicitly (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:1): "'until a priest stood up with Urim and Thummim' [Ezra 2:63]: and were there Urim and Thummim at that time? Rather, it is like a man who says to his fellow: until the dead live, until the son of David comes." Thus they testify of themselves that they sometimes speak with excessive exaggeration. The way of exaggeration is found among our ancients both in their speech and in their books. They had a fixed rule, when they explained ancient books or the words of sages who preceded them, not to take the words as they are written, for the language of the Torah and of the other Holy Writings and the words of the sages also sometimes use the way of hyperbole and exaggeration (Hullin 90a⚠1, and the places noted there). Now so too was the matter with respect to the attribution of the halakhot. As the periods of time went forward and moved further from the first generations, so they were the more stirred to hold to the principle that if we find halakhot whose nature and source we do not know, we should not try to find a far-fetched reason for them; rather, it is easier to attach the doubtful [halakhah] to a tradition from Sinai, for so it is with many halakhot that are embedded in the Mishnah and are doubtful to us. One of the greatest of the sages (R. Yoḥanan) set down the principle in a short but clear saying: "If a halakhah comes into your hand and you do not know its nature, do not push it off to another matter,⚠2 for many halakhot were said to Moses at Sinai, and all of them are embedded in the Mishnah" (Yerushalmi Pe'ah chapter 3⚠3). If we remember all the proofs and demonstrations brought above on the essence of tradition, we will see that this sage aimed at the truth. For it is true and clear that many matters of tradition must be attributed to a very ancient time, and all of them are embedded in the Mishnah; but it is not known how to distinguish between the degrees of their antiquity in time, because they were not recorded with an indication of their time, and they were also written and taught all in exactly one form. And now it has become clear to us that in truth it is so: from of old they believed that from the time of the giving and the writing of the Torah they had many matters, held orally, to explain what is obscure in the written Torah. But under the pressure of the hardships and troubles that befell them in almost every generation, and because of the various hindrances, material and moral, by which the tradition was held back in its course, many matters were forgotten and were as if they had never been. And even what remained alive and enduring in the practices of the people and in their customs did not remain in such a way that we could perceive from it its antiquity and its source. Only from the days of the Scribes did they begin to expound the Torah and to fix halakhot, new as well as old; and many turns and events passed over them until they brought the store of halakhot into a proper order. Even then they could not grasp their secret, to know which of the halakhot was received from an ancient time and which was new in the course of time, for the form of all of them was the same, and the marks of the received ones were not recognizable in them. Therefore it was a rule among them that all doubtful halakhot of this kind, about which they were in doubt from whom, when and for what reason they arose, they attached to the most ancient time, that is, to a tradition from Moses at Sinai.

2.note: Printed אחד ("one"); the Yerushalmi reads לדבר אחר ("another matter"); rendered by the sense.

3.note: Printed chapter 3; the saying of R. Yoḥanan is in Yerushalmi Pe'ah 2:4 (2:6 in some editions).

rows.en: But it is very strange that we have found no trace from the time of the generations of the Scribes that would hint at the foundation of the belief in an oral tradition from Sinai. This caused many to waver in their belief, for they thought that perhaps these ancients did not know of it and did not recognize it. For if they had believed in it, why did they keep silent and say nothing about it, since this view is a great principle for their activity, for their teaching and for the religion of the Jews in general? Would it not have been fitting for them to speak of it explicitly, as they spoke of other principles that are needed for strengthening the Torah, and commanded: "Be deliberate in judgment, raise up many students, and make a fence for the Torah" [Avot 1:1]? However, the lack of proclamation of this belief is no sign and proof of the lack of its existence. That they did not make their view on this known is only because in the generation of the Scribes the proclamation of their thought about tradition was simply superfluous, just as they did not warn, and were not forced to warn, about the belief in the divinity of the written Torah. For only a challenge from one side brings about the need to proclaim its opposite; and indeed in the days of the later generations the challenge was the cause of the proclamation of this belief. But in the days of the first period there was no one who challenged the matter, for the whole people returned willingly and with a desiring soul to the Torah, and no one cast doubt on what the Scribes or the men of understanding taught them, and no one asked, "Whence do they have this?" For they upheld and accepted everything upon themselves without hesitation. Therefore we cannot judge from their silence about the belief in this principle that it did not exist in their time. Indeed it is so without doubt that the foundation of this belief already existed in the nation in the generations of the first Scribes. From the years of generation after generation they knew that many statutes, ordinances and laws lived and endured in the nation only by tradition and were not written; some of them were written later or were hinted at (Zevaḥim 22a, and in many places), and most of them remained in the tradition. To this remnant were added statutes and limits to explain the Torah, which the Scribes and the sages of every generation newly made, and these too were only oral. And now, in the course of time and as events and hardships multiplied, the confusions grew and forgetfulness increased, and because of this the doubts also grew, so that they could not distinguish between what was truly received and what was new. Therefore the belief in an oral tradition from Sinai widened to include also explanations and statutes that were not received, until the later [sages] set down a rule (Sifra Beḥukotai chapter 8) that the Torah, its halakhot, its fine points and its explanations were given from Sinai; and that the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses the fine points of the Torah and the fine points of the Scribes. And they went beyond measure in saying (Berakhot 5a): Scripture, Mishnah and Gemara were all given to Moses from Sinai. Who can count all the sayings that show that the sages went in this line of thought? So this root made a branch and bore fruit in the course of time. However, if we look at the form of the derashot, which are the explanations, it will surely become clear to us, from the manner of presentation and the language they use in their derashot, that the derashot are their own explanations. For how could it enter the mind that if a man says "thus and thus I reason," or "the scripture comes to teach thus and thus," and another against him reasons or learns the opposite from the scripture, such derashot are received explanations and not their own explanations? Moreover, the sages sometimes said openly of some explanation that it was newly made at such and such a time (Yerushalmi Yevamot 5:3), and sometimes it is a common saying in their mouth: "the Scribes left me [room] and I will expound it" (Sotah 16a; Sifre Naso, piska 8). And if they said (Megillah 19b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moses what the Scribes would in future newly make, and believed (Yerushalmi Megillah 2:5 and Ḥagigah 1:1, and Midrash Kohelet) that even what a diligent student will in future teach was given to Moses at Sinai, for "there is nothing new under the sun" [Ecclesiastes 1:9], then it clearly follows from this that they held the midrashim of all the generations to be new, and nevertheless [said that] they were given to Moses at Sinai. And they said explicitly of the work of the Scribes that they founded the halakhah and made the halakhah new (Yerushalmi Eruvin 5:1). We find that they sometimes mention "explanations of Sinai" and "fine points of Sinai" (Sifra Beḥukotai chapter 8), and sometimes mention "explanations of the Scribes" (Sanhedrin 88b) and "fine points of the Scribes" (Sifra Kedoshim chapter 8, and Sanhedrin 87a). Likewise we find that the midrashim of the sages were called by them "matters written in the Torah" (Tosefta Hullin chapter 10), even a midrash that is not the meaning and the plain sense of the scripture. And of the commandment of reading the Megillah, which is an ordinance of the sages, they said in one place (Yerushalmi Megillah 7:6⚠1): "this scroll was said to Moses at Sinai"; and in another place they said that it is an ordinance of the sages, in contrast to the commandments of the Torah that were said to Moses at Sinai (Tosefta Sotah chapter 7⚠2; Shevu'ot 39a; and Nahmanides in his strictures on the *Sefer ha-Mitzvot*, root 1). Now if we compare all these sayings with one another, how many explicit contradictions shall we find in them? Where is the wonderful craftsman who can reconcile these denials? And where is the sound mind that can bear the opposites mentioned without saying this: if they said that what they newly made in all times was already given to Moses at Sinai, they did not say it precisely; rather, their intent was that all the new explanations lay within the statute of the Torah, and therefore they were of value as if they had been given from Sinai. And just as this was so with the explanations that were clearly new, so it is to be understood also with the doubtful explanations; and if so, what they said, that all the explanations were given from Sinai, is also not to be understood precisely and strictly.

1.note: Yerushalmi Megillah has only four chapters; the saying is in Yerushalmi Megillah 1:5 (70d). Kept as printed.

footnotes.en: These are the halakhot in the Mishnah. (Pe'ah 2:6): "Naḥum the Scribe said, etc.: a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai, that one who sows his field with two kinds of wheat, if he made them into one threshing floor, gives one pe'ah; two threshing floors, he gives two pe'ot." This halakhah was hidden from Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, who was Nasi; and if he did not know it, how can we say that it was agreed and well known? The second, in Eduyot (8:3⚠1): "R. Joshua said: I have a tradition from Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, etc., a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, that Elijah will not come to declare unclean or to declare clean." It is clear that he does not mean that Moses received at Sinai what Elijah will do in the future; that is a thing reason cannot bear. But in truth R. Joshua was repeating in this place his view that he made known in another place. That is, R. Joshua laid down a rule that from the day the Torah was given to Israel, they were given the authority to decide their doubts according to their view and according to the agreement of the majority, and "it is not in heaven" (Bava Metzia 59b). In a similar way he said here too that it is not Elijah's office to declare unclean or clean, for this is not the office of the prophets but the office of the sages, and the prophet has no power to change anything; but so it was decreed from Sinai that the sages should decide, that is, so it is set in the statute of the Torah. In this sense he uses the expression "a halakhah to Moses at Sinai," and this matter alone is enough to give us a correct picture of the meaning of this expression. See Maimonides' commentary there. The third, in Mishnah Yadayim (4:3): "a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, that Ammon and Moab give second tithe in the seventh year." It is a clear thing that this is not from Sinai and is not a law of the Torah; it is a late ordinance that the sages enacted. The Rosh already remarked on this in his commentary on tractate Yadayim, in the place mentioned, and in chapter 1 of Hilkhot Mikva'ot; and so wrote R. Simeon⚠2 of Sens in his commentary. See further Maimonides, Hilkhot Mattenot Aniyyim chapter 6, halakhah 1, and what the author of *Kesef Mishneh* wrote there.

1.note: The saying about Elijah is Eduyot 8:7; kept as printed.

2.note: Printed Shimon; the commentator on Zera'im and Tohorot is R. Samson (Shimshon) of Sens.

footnotes.en: In Torat Kohanim [Sifra], Tzav, chapter 11: "half a log of oil for the thank offering, and a quarter [log] of oil for the nazirite, and the eleven days between one menstrual period and the next are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai." R. Akiva disputes all three of them. In Niddah (73a) the reading is "a quarter of wine for the nazirite," and R. Akiva holds that there is no measure of a quarter for the nazirite (Nazir 34a); see there (38a), Tosafot s.v. nazir, and further there in the Yerushalmi, 5:5. The matter is made clear in the Tosefta that is cited in Tosafot Eruvin (4a), s.v. gefen. The reading of Tosafot in Niddah was "a quarter of oil" (not "a quarter of wine" as we have it), for if the reading of Tosafot had been "a quarter of wine," their words would have no meaning, since they said that R. Akiva disputes this too "even though we have not found it," whereas on the quarter of wine R. Akiva disputes explicitly. Therefore it is proven that their reading was "a quarter of oil," like the reading of Torat Kohanim before us. Be that as it may, R. Akiva disputes all three.

Tosefta Yadayim chapter 2 is a copy from the Mishnah. [Tosefta] Pe'ah chapter 2⚠1: "R. Ilai said: I asked R. Joshua about which sheaves the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel dispute" (that is, about a sheaf near the fence, Pe'ah 6:2); "he said to me: this teaching concerns the sheaf, etc. And I asked R. Eliezer, and he said to me: they agree about these; about what did they dispute? About the sheaf that he took hold of to bring to the town, etc. And when I set out the words before R. Eleazar ben Azariah, he said to me: [By] the covenant! These are the very words that were spoken to Moses at Horeb" (see the Yerushalmi and the commentary of R. Samson [of Sens]). Thus for R. Eleazar ben Azariah, that a sheaf near the fence is forgotten [produce] is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai. R. Z. Frankel, in *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 21, wrote: how can [this] apply to a dispute of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, that it should be a halakhah to Moses at Sinai? This is an error, for the dispute is not the halakhah; the halakhah is that a sheaf near the fence is forgotten [produce], and the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel never disputed about it. And in [Tosefta] Ḥallah chapter 1: "R. Eleazar said: I asked R. Joshua: the loaves of the thank offering and the wafers of the nazirite, what is their [law] concerning ḥallah? He said to me: they are exempt. And when I came and asked R. Eliezer, he said to me: if he made them for himself, they are exempt; to sell in the market, they are liable. And when I came and set out the words before R. Eleazar ben Azariah, he said to me: [By] the covenant! These are the words that were spoken to Moses at Horeb." Here in both cases R. Joshua disputes explicitly, and in the words of R. Eleazar ben Azariah too there is nothing to decide whether he said so absolutely or by way of wonder, that is: are the words of R. Eliezer then words from Sinai? (see Pesaḥim 38b). And the author of the Mishnah himself ruled without attribution like R. Joshua; necessarily this halakhah was not received with clarity. In Ḥullin (42a): "eighteen terefot were said to Moses at Sinai"; and in the Mishnah it is said: "whatever is not like it cannot live," and it is not their way to give a sign and a reason for a halakhah to Moses at Sinai. In Menaḥot (35b) and in many places: "Our Rabbis taught: square tefillin are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai." Shabbat (79b) has two halakhot: tefillin on parchment (kelaf) and a mezuzah on dukhsustos; and there is a Tanna there who holds that if he changed in this or in that, it is valid. How is that possible with a halakhah to Moses at Sinai? Was the halakhah not taught without qualification, and whence the distinction between the [ideal] commandment and what is indispensable? Yerushalmi Megillah 1:9 has eleven halakhot: tefillin are written with ink, and lines are scored, and they are wrapped with hair, and hung with a cloth, and stuck with glue, and sewn with sinews, and so for all that is sewn, and one leaves [space] between line and line, between letter and letter, between column and column, and one leaves a margin above and below. In Sukkah (44a) there are three halakhot: the ten saplings, the willow and the water libation; and they did not agree on this, for some say that the willow and the water libation are a law of the Torah, and some say that they are an institution of the prophets (Yerushalmi there). In Yerushalmi Megillah 6:9⚠2: "the [final letters] mem, nun, tsadi, pe, kaf, the Seers said them, a halakhah to Moses at Sinai," and others dispute. Niddah (45a): [a girl] younger than three years (who was violated⚠3) is fit for the priesthood. This is not so in the view of R. Akiva, for in his view it is from reasoning, since he distinguishes between [a girl who] has experienced intercourse and one who has not. And his students, who answered him, "just as the whole Torah is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, so is this," did not say so absolutely; rather, because they did not know the reason for the matter, and the reason of R. Akiva did not seem good in their eyes, they said: why do we need to push to a far-fetched reason? Is it not better to say that it is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, as people are accustomed to say of the whole Torah when we do not know the reason of things and their source? Now of these twenty there remain for us only twelve, concerning the tefillin, on which no one disputes.

footnotes.en: In Eruvin (4a) it is said in the name of Rav: measures, partitions and interpositions are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai. And likewise R. Yoḥanan said: measures and punishments are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai (Yoma 80a). Some dispute about the measures and about the measures of punishments (Eruvin and Yoma there, and Sukkah 6a), and some say that the sages stated all the measures (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 1:1). And we learned in Torat Kohanim, Shemini, chapter 7, on the impurity of a creeping thing: the sages measured it at the size of a lentil. And for the other measures that are not specified there in the Gemara we always find "the sages measured" (Sifre Beha'alotekha, piska 49; Ki Tetze, [piska] 222; Tosefta Bava Metzia chapter 2; and in many places). Interpositions too are not the view of all, for they asked in the Gemara: are interpositions [a law] of the Torah? And although he tried to answer, his intent is only to settle the view of the one who says [it is a] halakhah. And they said: by the law of the Torah, [an interposition over] most of it and about which one is particular interposes (Sukkah 6a, and in many places). How the expression "a law of the Torah" is mostly explained, see Yerushalmi Sukkah 4:1 and in many places. And about partitions too some dispute in the Gemara (Sukkah there). In Menaḥot (35a): the titura of the tefillin; there and in Eruvin (97a): the knot of the tefillin; in Shabbat (62a): the shin of the tefillin (and see there in Tosafot, and Eruvin 96a and Tosafot); in Menaḥot (35a): the ma'abarta of the tefillin. On these four, concerning tefillin, no one in the Gemara disputes. In Sanhedrin (82a): "one who has intercourse with an Aramean woman, zealots may strike him"; whoever looks there will see that the whole saying there is only words of aggadah. Kiddushin (39a): orlah outside the Land; and there is a dispute about it in the Gemara. Menaḥot (35a): black straps; but see there in the Gemara, where it is made clear that several ancients did not practise so, and they strain to explain the view of the one who says that it is a halakhah. In Nedarim (37a⚠1): the scribal reading, the scribal omission, [words] read but not written, written but not read, are a halakhah to Moses at Sinai. See above, chapter 7, where I showed what the nature of this halakhah is. In Menaḥot (32a): the scoring of a mezuzah is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai; but whoever looks in Megillah (18b) will find that some dispute this halakhah. Thus among all those that the Amoraim mentioned there are only four halakhot on which no one disputes. In sum, all the halakhot on which there is no dispute are only sixteen in number.

1.note: The passage on mikra soferim etc. is Nedarim 37b; the scan shows a point (side a). Kept as printed.

footnotes.en: "Halakhah" without more: circumcision overrides the Sabbath (Shabbat 132a); the females of an Egyptian and of an Edomite are permitted (Yevamot 76a); a man may impose naziriteship on his son, but a woman may not (Nazir 28a); a man may shave [with the offerings] of his father's naziriteship (there 30a); unspecified money falls to the freewill offering (there 25a); a bone the size of a barley grain defiles (there 57b); covering the blood [may be done] with anything; a nazirite who shaved is liable [whatever he shaved] with anything that shaves; a get may be written on anything (Sotah 16a). In all of them the commentators explained [it as] a halakhah to Moses at Sinai, but I did not find it so stated explicitly in the Gemara. But I found that the halakhah "an Ammonite man and not an Ammonite woman" is a halakhah that was newly made (Yerushalmi Yevamot 3:3⚠1), and the same holds for Egyptian and Edomite females. If you look at all the places I have indicated, you will find that in most of them there is a dispute.

footnotes.en: Hilkheta gemiri: the impurity of the deep (Pesaḥim 81b); half damage for pebbles (Bava Kamma 3b); doubtful impurity (Ḥullin 9b); the covering-stone and the side-stone (there 72b); and further in many places. The phrase gemiri is not [a] halakhah to Moses at Sinai; the proof is from Sanhedrin (101b): "we have it by tradition that there is no sitting in the Temple court except for the kings of the house of David"; and see *Tosafot Yom Tov*, Zevaḥim 1:3. And in Pesaḥim (52a) Rashi explained gemiri: a tradition from the fathers.

From Mishnah Shabbat 1:2⚠1 and Terumot 2:1 it is proven that "in truth they said" is not a halakhah to Moses at Sinai; see Bertinoro and *Tosafot Yom Tov*. Rashi explained in Bava Metzia (60a): every "in truth they said" is a halakhah, and one is not to hesitate or stammer about the matter. There in Bava Metzia it says only "halakhah" without more, and in Shabbat (92a) a baraita is brought whose reading is also "halakhah" without more. But in the Yerushalmi the reading in several places is "every 'in truth they said' is a halakhah to Moses at Sinai"; and these words "to Moses at Sinai" are only a gloss from the margin that some corrector added, and some copyist who was not expert brought them into the text.
